evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RhoA has been implicated in mitotic rounding.
source: RhoA, another of the major small GTPases, has been implicated in mitosis (Chircop, 2014), mitotic rounding (Maddox and Burridge, 2003; Matthews et al., 2012) and cell-in-cell formation (Overholtzer et al., 2007) through previous studies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RhoA has been implicated in cell-in-cell formation.
source: RhoA, another of the major small GTPases, has been implicated in mitosis (Chircop, 2014), mitotic rounding (Maddox and Burridge, 2003; Matthews et al., 2012) and cell-in-cell formation (Overholtzer et al., 2007) through previous studies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Control 16HBE cells show a relatively low level of RhoA activity during metaphase.
source: While control 16HBE cells show a relatively low level of RhoA activity during metaphase, a clear enrichment of active RhoA is frequently observed at the metaphase cortex among Cdc42-depleted cells (37%; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: A clear enrichment of active RhoA is frequently observed at the metaphase cortex among Cdc42-depleted cells (37%).
source: While control 16HBE cells show a relatively low level of RhoA activity during metaphase, a clear enrichment of active RhoA is frequently observed at the metaphase cortex among Cdc42-depleted cells (37%; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: An increase in cortical actin can be observed among Cdc42-depleted, metaphase cells.
source: Related to this, an increase in cortical actin can also be observed among Cdc42-depleted, metaphase cells (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Cdc42 constrains mitotic RhoA activation in polarised epithelial cells.
source: Together, these data indicate that Cdc42 constrains mitotic RhoA activation in polarised epithelial cells, and accordingly, that loss of Cdc42 permits overactivation of cortical RhoA during metaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RhoA activity data.

claim: Loss of Cdc42 permits overactivation of cortical RhoA during metaphase.
source: Together, these data indicate that Cdc42 constrains mitotic RhoA activation in polarised epithelial cells, and accordingly, that loss of Cdc42 permits overactivation of cortical RhoA during metaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RhoA activity data.

claim: Inhibition of the Rho proteins has a clear impact on mitotic spreading, yielding a significant increase in basal area.
source: Although mitotic cells do remain somewhat rounded in the presence of this toxin, inhibition of the Rho proteins has a clear impact on mitotic spreading, yielding a significant increase in basal area, and thus partially reversing the effect of Cdc42-depletion (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Inhibition of the Rho proteins partially reverses the effect of Cdc42-depletion on mitotic spreading.
source: Although mitotic cells do remain somewhat rounded in the presence of this toxin, inhibition of the Rho proteins has a clear impact on mitotic spreading, yielding a significant increase in basal area, and thus partially reversing the effect of Cdc42-depletion (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: RhoA activity has been implicated in mitotic cell retraction, rigidity and rounding.
source: These data are consistent with previous studies that have implicated RhoA activity in mitotic cell retraction, rigidity and rounding (Maddox and Burridge, 2003; Matthews et al., 2012), along with its targets ROCK (Maddox and Burridge, 2003; Meyer et al., 2011) and myosin (Matthews et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ROCK has been implicated in mitotic cell retraction, rigidity and rounding.
source: These data are consistent with previous studies that have implicated RhoA activity in mitotic cell retraction, rigidity and rounding (Maddox and Burridge, 2003; Matthews et al., 2012), along with its targets ROCK (Maddox and Burridge, 2003; Meyer et al., 2011) and myosin (Matthews et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Myosin has been implicated in mitotic cell retraction, rigidity and rounding.
source: These data are consistent with previous studies that have implicated RhoA activity in mitotic cell retraction, rigidity and rounding (Maddox and Burridge, 2003; Matthews et al., 2012), along with its targets ROCK (Maddox and Burridge, 2003; Meyer et al., 2011) and myosin (Matthews et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Suppression of ROCK activity rescued mitotic cell spreading in Cdc42-depleted cells.
source: To explore this observation further, live Cdc42-depleted cells were treated with additional pathway inhibitors, and suppression of ROCK (Y-27632) or myosin (blebbistatin) activity similarly rescued mitotic cell spreading in Cdc42-depleted cells (Figure 4d–e).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4d-e.

claim: Suppression of myosin activity rescued mitotic cell spreading in Cdc42-depleted cells.
source: To explore this observation further, live Cdc42-depleted cells were treated with additional pathway inhibitors, and suppression of ROCK (Y-27632) or myosin (blebbistatin) activity similarly rescued mitotic cell spreading in Cdc42-depleted cells (Figure 4d–e).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4d-e.

claim: Aberrant activation of a Rho/ROCK/myosin cascade during mitosis can drive enhanced retraction and rounding.
source: Together, these data indicate that aberrant activation of a Rho/ROCK/myosin cascade during mitosis can drive enhanced retraction and rounding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Rap1 is known to control post-mitotic spreading.
source: Rap1 is yet another small GTPase, which, importantly here, is known to control post-mitotic spreading (Dao et al., 2009; Lancaster et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Expression of DN-Rap1 reduces spreading and increases rounding during 16HBE division.
source: Consistent with this, we confirm that expression of DN-Rap1 reduces spreading and increases rounding during 16HBE division (Figure 5a–d).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 5a-d.

claim: Inhibition of Rap1 induces adherent entosis.
source: Strikingly, inhibition of Rap1, like Cdc42, also induces adherent entosis, albeit at a lower level.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Cell-in-cell formation among Rap1-inhibited cells occurs during or shortly after mitosis.
source: Cell-in-cell formation among Rap1-inhibited cells occurs during or shortly after mitosis (Figure 5e–g, Video 6) and is inhibited by G2 arrest (Cdk1i).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 5e-g and Video 6.

claim: Cell-in-cell formation among Rap1-inhibited cells is inhibited by G2 arrest.
source: Cell-in-cell formation among Rap1-inhibited cells occurs during or shortly after mitosis (Figure 5e–g, Video 6) and is inhibited by G2 arrest (Cdk1i).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Enhanced mitotic deadhesion and rounding drive subsequent cell-in-cell formation.
source: These data are consistent with a model in which enhanced mitotic deadhesion and rounding drive subsequent cell-in-cell formation.
evidence: This is presented as a model consistent with the data.

claim: Detached interphase cells undergo efficient entosis in suspension (~8%).
source: Strikingly, while detached interphase cells undergo efficient entosis in suspension (~8%), penetration of adherent hosts is barely detectable.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Penetration of adherent hosts by detached interphase cells is barely detectable.
source: Strikingly, while detached interphase cells undergo efficient entosis in suspension (~8%), penetration of adherent hosts is barely detectable.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Simple loss of matrix-attachment is insufficient to drive penetration of an adherent host.
source: These data indicate that simple loss of matrix-attachment is insufficient to drive penetration of an adherent host.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Entosis has not been observed among 16HBE-monolayers upon depletion of matrix-adhesion proteins (e.g. β1-integrin).
source: Consistent with this, entosis has not been observed among 16HBE-monolayers upon depletion of matrix-adhesion proteins (e.g. β1-integrin; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mitotic deadhesion and rounding can drive the entotic penetration of an adherent host cell, while matrix-detachment during interphase cannot.
source: Together, these data indicate that mitotic deadhesion and rounding, which can be augmented by inhibition of Cdc42 or Rap1, can drive the entotic penetration of an adherent host cell, while matrix-detachment during interphase cannot.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There are important mechanistic differences between cell cannibalism under detached and adherent conditions.
source: These findings infer important mechanistic differences between cell cannibalism under detached and adherent conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The distinctive biophysical changes associated with mitosis are an essential requirement when entosis occurs in an adherent host.
source: We conclude that the distinctive biophysical changes associated with mitosis are an essential requirement when entosis occurs in an adherent host.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: MCF7 (breast) and HCT116 (colorectal) cells undergo adherent entosis under basal conditions.
source: Interestingly, MCF7 (breast) and HCT116 (colorectal) cells were found to undergo adherent entosis under basal conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Cell-in-cell formation in MCF7 and HCT116 cells is coincident with cell division.
source: Importantly, cell-in-cell formation is coincident with cell division, as shown by timelapse microscopy (Figure 6a–b, Videos 7–8), and is largely dependent on progression through mitosis, in both 2D and 3D culture (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6a-d and Videos 7-8.

claim: Cell-in-cell formation in MCF7 and HCT116 cells is largely dependent on progression through mitosis, in both 2D and 3D culture.
source: Importantly, cell-in-cell formation is coincident with cell division, as shown by timelapse microscopy (Figure 6a–b, Videos 7–8), and is largely dependent on progression through mitosis, in both 2D and 3D culture (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6c-d.

claim: Mitosis drives constitutive adherent entosis in certain transformed tumour cell lines.
source: These data indicate that mitosis drives constitutive adherent entosis in certain transformed tumour cell lines and raise the interesting possibility that cell division may promote cell cannibalism in the proliferative environment of a tumour.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Cell division may promote cell cannibalism in the proliferative environment of a tumour.
source: These data indicate that mitosis drives constitutive adherent entosis in certain transformed tumour cell lines and raise the interesting possibility that cell division may promote cell cannibalism in the proliferative environment of a tumour.
evidence: This is presented as a possibility raised by the findings.

claim: 31/75 ductal carcinomas were positive for entosis.
source: 31/75 ductal carcinomas were positive for entosis, and among these, mitotic activity positively correlates with cell-in-cell formation, with statistical significance (Figure 6g).
evidence: This is a finding from the tissue microarray analysis.

claim: Among entosis-positive ductal carcinomas, mitotic activity positively correlates with cell-in-cell formation, with statistical significance.
source: 31/75 ductal carcinomas were positive for entosis, and among these, mitotic activity positively correlates with cell-in-cell formation, with statistical significance (Figure 6g).
evidence: This is a finding from the tissue microarray analysis shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Mitosis may drive entotic cell-in-cell formation in vivo.
source: These data are consistent with the notion that mitosis may drive entotic cell-in-cell formation in vivo.
evidence: This is presented as a notion consistent with the tissue microarray data.

claim: Cell death is the predominant fate for internalised cells following mitotic entosis.
source: Similar to suspension conditions, cell death is the predominant fate for internalised cells following mitotic entosis, which can occur by either non-apoptotic and apoptotic means (Figure 6h–i).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6h-i.

claim: Internalised cell death following mitotic entosis can occur by either non-apoptotic and apoptotic means.
source: Similar to suspension conditions, cell death is the predominant fate for internalised cells following mitotic entosis, which can occur by either non-apoptotic and apoptotic means (Figure 6h–i).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6h-i.

claim: Host cells are more frequently multi-nucleated than surrounding single cells.
source: Again, similar to suspension entosis, host cells are more frequently multi-nucleated than surrounding single cells, suggesting that abscission can be disrupted by entosis in adherent, as well as matrix-detached, conditions (Figure 6j–k).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6j-k.

claim: Abscission can be disrupted by entosis in adherent, as well as matrix-detached, conditions.
source: Again, similar to suspension entosis, host cells are more frequently multi-nucleated than surrounding single cells, suggesting that abscission can be disrupted by entosis in adherent, as well as matrix-detached, conditions (Figure 6j–k).
evidence: This is presented as a suggestion based on the finding of increased multinucleation in host cells.

claim: Mitosis-induced entosis occurs basally in adherent cancer cell lines and human breast carcinomas.
source: Together, these data establish that mitosis-induced entosis occurs basally in adherent cancer cell lines and human breast carcinomas.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Mitosis-induced entosis can drive inner cell killing, a potentially tumour suppressive effect.
source: Mitosis-induced entosis can drive inner cell killing, a potentially tumour suppressive effect, but also promotes host cell multi-nucleation, a route to tumour-promoting genomic instability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Mitosis-induced entosis promotes host cell multi-nucleation, a route to tumour-promoting genomic instability.
source: Mitosis-induced entosis can drive inner cell killing, a potentially tumour suppressive effect, but also promotes host cell multi-nucleation, a route to tumour-promoting genomic instability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Taxanes can induce prometaphase arrest, multipolar division and cell death.
source: Many cancers are treated chemotherapeutically with taxanes (e.g. Paclitaxel), which can induce prometaphase arrest, multipolar division and cell death (Zasadil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Taxol treatment increases mitotic index in 16HBE cells.
source: As expected, taxol treatment increases mitotic index under these conditions, arresting the cells in prometaphase (in contrast to Cdk1i which arrests at G2/M, inhibiting entry into mitosis).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Taxol treatment arrests cells in prometaphase.
source: As expected, taxol treatment increases mitotic index under these conditions, arresting the cells in prometaphase (in contrast to Cdk1i which arrests at G2/M, inhibiting entry into mitosis).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Taxol treatment consistently increases cell-in-cell formation in 16HBE cells.
source: Importantly, taxol treatment also consistently increases cell-in-cell formation under these conditions, in line with an induction of mitotic entosis.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Nocodazole (microtubule assembly inhibitor) can phenocopy the effect of taxol on cell-in-cell formation.
source: This effect can be phenocopied with additional drugs that inhibit mitotic progression through different mechanisms, including nocodazole (microtubule assembly inhibitor) and STLC (mitotic kinesin inhibitor), suggesting that entosis occurs as a consequence of prometaphase arrest rather than microtubule stabilisation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: STLC (mitotic kinesin inhibitor) can phenocopy the effect of taxol on cell-in-cell formation.
source: This effect can be phenocopied with additional drugs that inhibit mitotic progression through different mechanisms, including nocodazole (microtubule assembly inhibitor) and STLC (mitotic kinesin inhibitor), suggesting that entosis occurs as a consequence of prometaphase arrest rather than microtubule stabilisation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Entosis occurs as a consequence of prometaphase arrest rather than microtubule stabilisation.
source: This effect can be phenocopied with additional drugs that inhibit mitotic progression through different mechanisms, including nocodazole (microtubule assembly inhibitor) and STLC (mitotic kinesin inhibitor), suggesting that entosis occurs as a consequence of prometaphase arrest rather than microtubule stabilisation.
evidence: This is presented as a suggestion based on the finding that different drugs with different mechanisms all induce entosis.

claim: Taxol, nocodazole and STLC significantly enhance mitotic deadhesion and rounding.
source: Strikingly, we also find that taxol, nocodazole and STLC significantly enhance mitotic deadhesion and rounding (Figure 7d–f), thus independently supporting the model that changes in mitotic morphology are closely associated with adherent cell-in-cell formation.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 7d-f.

claim: Changes in mitotic morphology are closely associated with adherent cell-in-cell formation.
source: Strikingly, we also find that taxol, nocodazole and STLC significantly enhance mitotic deadhesion and rounding (Figure 7d–f), thus independently supporting the model that changes in mitotic morphology are closely associated with adherent cell-in-cell formation.
evidence: This is presented as a model supported by the drug treatment data.

claim: In both cultured MCF7 cells and mouse xenograft models, 24 hr taxol treatment promotes a significant increase in mitotic index.
source: In both cultured cells (Figure 7g–h) and mouse xenograft models (Figure 7i–l), 24 hr taxol treatment promotes a significant increase in mitotic index, and a corresponding induction of cell-in-cell formation, consistent with mitosis-induced entosis.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 7g-l.

claim: In both cultured MCF7 cells and mouse xenograft models, 24 hr taxol treatment promotes a corresponding induction of cell-in-cell formation.
source: In both cultured cells (Figure 7g–h) and mouse xenograft models (Figure 7i–l), 24 hr taxol treatment promotes a significant increase in mitotic index, and a corresponding induction of cell-in-cell formation, consistent with mitosis-induced entosis.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 7g-l.

claim: Taxol is reported to inhibit MCF7 entosis in suspension.
source: Notably, as taxol is reported to inhibit MCF7 entosis in suspension (Xia et al., 2014), these data further suggest that the mechanisms of detached versus adherent cell-in-cell formation are quite distinct.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The mechanisms of detached versus adherent cell-in-cell formation are quite distinct.
source: Notably, as taxol is reported to inhibit MCF7 entosis in suspension (Xia et al., 2014), these data further suggest that the mechanisms of detached versus adherent cell-in-cell formation are quite distinct.
evidence: This is presented as a suggestion based on the contrasting effects of taxol on suspension versus adherent entosis.

claim: Taxane treatment enhances mitotic deadhesion and rounding and promotes cell cannibalism through entosis.
source: Together, our findings establish that taxane treatment enhances mitotic deadhesion and rounding and promotes cell cannibalism through entosis, and reinforce the conclusion that changes in mitotic morphology can drive adherent entosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There are at least two mechanistic routes to entosis: loss of matrix-attachment and cell division.
source: In conclusion, we propose that there are at least two mechanistic routes to entosis: loss of matrix-attachment and cell division.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: Anchorage independence and unrestrained proliferation are two classic hallmarks of cancer.
source: It is striking that anchorage independence and unrestrained proliferation, two classic hallmarks of cancer (Freedman and Shin, 1974; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011), can both drive this form of cell cannibalism, so commonly observed in tumours.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Anchorage independence and unrestrained proliferation can both drive entosis.
source: It is striking that anchorage independence and unrestrained proliferation, two classic hallmarks of cancer (Freedman and Shin, 1974; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011), can both drive this form of cell cannibalism, so commonly observed in tumours.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Mitotic index is one of the key criteria used to stage breast cancers.
source: Importantly, as mitotic index is one of the key criteria used to stage breast cancers, our findings can in part explain the increased frequency of cell-in-cell structures among higher grade, more proliferative tumours (Krajcovic et al., 2011; Gupta and Dey, 2003; Abodief et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as known information about breast cancer staging.

claim: The findings can in part explain the increased frequency of cell-in-cell structures among higher grade, more proliferative tumours.
source: Importantly, as mitotic index is one of the key criteria used to stage breast cancers, our findings can in part explain the increased frequency of cell-in-cell structures among higher grade, more proliferative tumours (Krajcovic et al., 2011; Gupta and Dey, 2003; Abodief et al., 2006).
evidence: This is presented as an explanation based on the findings and citations to previous work.

claim: Cell-in-cell formation correlates with more aggressive disease.
source: Our study thus contributes new insights into the field of cell cannibalism in cancer, building on the emerging notion that cell-in-cell formation correlates with more aggressive disease (Krajcovic et al., 2011) and may provide prognostic indications (Schwegler et al., 2015; Schenker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cell-in-cell formation may provide prognostic indications.
source: Our study thus contributes new insights into the field of cell cannibalism in cancer, building on the emerging notion that cell-in-cell formation correlates with more aggressive disease (Krajcovic et al., 2011) and may provide prognostic indications (Schwegler et al., 2015; Schenker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Paclitaxel enhances mitotic deadhesion and rounding, thereby driving subsequent cell-in-cell formation through entosis.
source: Interestingly, we find that Paclitaxel enhances mitotic deadhesion and rounding, thereby driving subsequent cell-in-cell formation through entosis.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: There is a significant debate regarding the mechanism of action of taxane-family drugs.
source: There is a significant debate regarding the mechanism of action of taxane-family drugs (Weaver, 2014), which can cause prometaphase arrest, multipolar divisions and cell death (Zasadil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The outcome of entosis is broadly conserved, whether it is triggered by deadhesion or mitosis, within an adherent or detached host cell.
source: Finally, we show that the outcome of entosis is broadly conserved, whether it is triggered by deadhesion or mitosis, within an adherent or detached host cell (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Aberrantly dividing cells may penetrate, and be eliminated by, the surrounding normal epithelium, in a tumour-suppressive act of 'assisted suicide'.
source: We find here that the host cell can be wild-type and fully adherent, developing an intriguing model in which aberrantly dividing cells may penetrate, and be eliminated by, the surrounding normal epithelium, in a tumour-suppressive act of 'assisted suicide'.
evidence: This is presented as a model developed from the findings.

claim: One aberrant division may promote more aberrant divisions, thereby contributing to tumour progression.
source: In this case, an alternative model emerges in which one aberrant division promotes more, thereby contributing to tumour progression.
evidence: This is presented as an alternative model based on the findings.
